messages.subject: bad item fit
parts:
Hi Phil, 

I have a quick question on item fit.
I have a polytomous (7 response option) data set with 10 items. 
They are unidimensional in nature. I used the Rasch item type to run the model.
The model can converge. There is no local dependency. The M2 statistics return an error, but I found out that it is because of too many intercepts (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/mirt-package/8bNbOJ8OukE). 
However, the p.S_X2 were more or less all quite bad. 
Is this because of sparseness? 
If it is, collapsing the response options the only way to remedy this problem? 

       item    S_X2 df.S_X2 p.S_X2

2   qns4     246.035     158  0.000

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: bad item fit
parts:
Hi Aiden,

More than likely these misfitting items are due to choosing a less flexible IRT model and less to do with sparse response categories. If you choose something more flexible, which are potentially more representative of the probabilistic relationship with the latent trait, then you'll likely notice large improvements in the item-fit statistics. HTH.

Phil

messages.author: 6a75f6f91a59c568
messages.subject: Re: bad item fit
parts:
Dr Kang, An author of the polytomous S-X2 index (Kang & Chen, 2007; Kang & Chen, 2008), commented personally in his lecture (Kang, Personal communication, 2016).

"The generalised partial credit model may appropriate in so many situations if you do not care the ideal-point (GGUM) model to measure typical performance."

Consider the best polytomous model which explain your data well what S-X2 fit could be neat (Kang, Personal communication, 2016). I agree with Phil. Sometimes the Rasch model seems too strict under the MMLE.

In addition, seven-point rating options too much. In many cases, Yes or No is enough.

Chernyshenko, O. S., Stark, S., Chan, K.-Y., Drasgow, F., & Williams, B. (2001). Fitting Item Response Theory Models to Two Personality Inventories: Issues and Insights. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 36(4), 523–562. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327906MBR3604_03

Wakita, T., Ueshima, N., & Noguchi, H. (2012). Psychological Distance Between Categories in the Likert Scale: Comparing Different Numbers of Options. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 72(4), 533–546. https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164411431162

Best,
Seongho
